title: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Chains of interaction link distant species' abundances

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Very different organisms are linked by chains of interaction, so that the abundance of one species can determine the frequency of another through intermediate species; for example, cats may control the frequency of red clover and heartsease by way of field-mice and humble-bees.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: On the Origin of Species by Means of Natural Selection, or the Preservation of Favoured Races in the Struggle for Life

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Hence it is quite credible that the presence of a feline animal in large numbers in a district might determine, through the intervention first of mice and then of bees, the frequency of certain flowers in that district!

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci Origin of Species claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Charles Darwin, On the Origin of Species (1st ed., London: John Murray, 1859), Chapter III, “Struggle for Existence”; section “Complex relations of all animals and plants throughout nature”. Scope: terrestrial communities of plants, pollinators, and their predators

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on darwin1859-ch03-10: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.64

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Interaction networks and community time series identify candidate chains, and some trophic cascades have open experimental data. The specific complete causal sequence is rarely observed at suitable resolution.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Fit a mediated causal model in systems with predator, intermediate consumer, pollinator and plant abundance time series, testing whether predator changes propagate through the specified links to plant frequency. A significant signed indirect effect supports the chain.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Interaction records rarely align with abundance through time.

Shared environmental drivers can mimic cascades.

discriminating power: 0.67

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: Open interaction networks can show multi-step links among dissimilar organisms, which supports the existential reading that abundance effects can travel through intermediates. Quantitative frequency control is present in only a minority of networks. The analysis is feasible for well-resolved webs and does not cover terrestrial communities at the scope of the example.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Trace indirect paths in interaction networks and, where abundance data exist, estimate whether changing one species' abundance predicts another's through an intermediate. Documented indirect effects would support the possibility of such chains; a systematic absence of indirect paths from predators to plants via seed predators or pollinators would count against the general mechanism.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
The cat-mouse-bee-clover example is more specific than the global interaction tables can reconstruct for one district.

A chain that is possible on a graph may be dynamically unimportant.

Most interaction records are presence of a link, not an effect on abundance.
